title: Event Triggered Execution: Change Default File Association
shortTitle: Event Triggered Execution: Change Default File Association
summary: Windows decides which program opens a file from the file name extension, and those mappings live in the registry. An extension such as .txt is listed under HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT, and its default value names a handler class; the handler class then holds one or more action keys under its shell subkey, and each action has a command subkey whose value is the command line Windows runs. The common actions are open, print, and printto, and the open action is what a double click uses. An attacker with write access to these keys, which in practice means writing to HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT or the underlying HKEY_CURRENT_USER or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE class keys, can repoint an action so their program runs every time a file of that type is opened. This is persistence without a service, a task, or a startup shortcut: the trigger is an ordinary user action and the malicious process is spawned by explorer.exe or the shell, so process ancestry points at legitimate components. Detection works best by comparing the recorded command lines for common extensions against a known good baseline, then checking the age, location, and signature of the named executable. Legitimate changes do occur during software installation, so the analyst looks for associations rewritten to unusual paths, unusual interpreters, or executables with no publisher, especially when the file type is one that many users open every day.

beginner.definition: When you open a file, Windows checks the part of its name after the dot, such as .txt, and then starts the program registered for that type. Those registrations are stored in a settings database called the registry. This technique is when an attacker changes a registration so their program runs instead.
beginner.whyItMatters: The attacker's program then runs whenever someone opens that kind of file, which can happen many times a day. Nothing needs to start at boot, so a check of startup items may show nothing wrong. The file still opens normally, so the user has no reason to be suspicious. It is a quiet way to keep running.
howItWorks: Windows keeps a list that maps each file name extension to a handler class.
Each handler class stores actions such as open and print under its shell key.
Under each action, a command key holds the exact command line that Windows runs.
The attacker edits that command value so it starts their program as well as the real one.
When a user double clicks a file of that type, Windows runs the attacker's command.
The process starts as a child of the normal Windows shell, so it looks legitimate.
beginner.example: Picture a shared kitchen where each shelf is labelled for a type of food, and a card tells you which tin opener to use. Someone swaps one card for another, so that opening a tin of beans now also unlocks a cupboard. You still get your beans, so you never question the card. The cupboard opens quietly each time you cook.
takeaways: File associations are registry mappings that decide which program opens which file type.
Changing one makes the attacker's code run each time a user opens that file type.
Confirm the registered handler is a program you know and expect, then check its signature.

objectives: Explain how Windows resolves a file name extension to a program.
Describe the registry path from extension to handler to command.
Explain why this persistence survives without startup entries or scheduled tasks.
Explain why the malicious process appears to come from the shell.
Describe how to baseline file associations and spot a tampered one.
